notes: The opening repeats the end of 2 Chronicles, but Ezra continues the proclamation. Its wording is retained where shared.
The final Jerusalem phrase can describe God here, or be connected back to his house.
Some vessel names are uncertain. The itemized figures total 2,499; verse 11 gives 5,400. Both are retained. “Of a second kind” in verse 10 is also uncertain.
vocabulary: The inner life and resolve of a person; here God stirs someone to act.

notes: Nehemiah 7 preserves a parallel register with differences in names and numbers. This chapter retains Ezra’s own entries and totals.
Names shared with later figures do not by themselves establish that they are the same people.
Shalmai, Meunim, and Nephusim follow the Hebrew reading tradition recorded alongside the written text.
The missing records concern eligibility for priestly service. The governor leaves the question open pending priestly discernment.
The stated assembly total is preserved without adjusting it to the itemized counts.
vocabulary: The Nethinim, a group assigned to service at the temple.
Sacred means associated with a priest’s inquiry for divine guidance; their precise form and operation are uncertain.
A daric was a gold coin; a mina was a unit of weight. The ancient units are retained.

notes: The Hebrew links building the altar with fear of surrounding peoples. It can also be understood as building despite that fear.
The Hebrew says “Judah” here. The related family designation in 2:40 is “Hodaviah.” The difference is retained.
The text describes weeping and joy together but does not explain every person’s reason for weeping.
vocabulary: An offering burned on the altar for God.
The autumn festival involving temporary shelters, also called Booths or Tabernacles.
Hebrew hesed: enduring loyalty and kindness in a relationship.

notes: “To him” follows the recorded Hebrew reading tradition. The written form is “not.”

Verses 6–23 collect later examples of opposition to Jerusalem under Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes. Verse 24 returns to the temple work under Darius. The letters about the city’s walls should not be mistaken for a continuous chronology of the temple project.
The biblical text switches from Hebrew to Aramaic at 4:8 and continues in Aramaic through 6:18.
Several group names are uncertain and may represent peoples or administrative groups. “Dahae” follows the recorded read form; the written form can be understood as “who are.”
The expression rendered “royal revenue” is uncertain; the sentence warns of financial harm to the king.
Eating the palace’s salt expresses dependence on, and an obligation of loyalty to, the king.
vocabulary: The Persian province west of the Euphrates, viewed from the empire’s eastern center.
Three kinds of royal payment; the exact distinctions between these terms are uncertain.

notes: The architectural term rendered “structure” is uncertain; it has also been understood as wall or woodwork.

The Aramaic says “we,” creating an abrupt change of voice. It is retained here. Some readings take the sentence as a report of the builders’ answer about their names; others understand the officials’ question, as in 5:9–10.
The term rendered “officials” may instead name a people or group.
“Temple” in Babylon can also be understood as “palace.”
Sheshbazzar’s role is reported here without equating him with Zerubbabel. The elders’ summary is retained alongside the earlier account of interrupted work.
vocabulary: An image of attentive care and protection.
The elders’ title for the God they serve; the letter preserves their own answer.

notes: The foundation and construction wording is difficult. The text gives height and width of sixty cubits each, but no length here. “New timber” follows the source’s vocalized wording.
The decree threatens impalement on a beam taken from the offender’s own house. This is the king’s stated penalty.
Artaxerxes is named here as well as Cyrus and Darius, although verse 15 dates the temple’s completion to Darius. The retrospective list is retained.
The text returns to Hebrew here.
The verse includes others who joined the returned exiles to seek the LORD. It does not explicitly identify their ancestry.
The source calls the ruler “king of Assyria” here. The title is retained even though the surrounding narrative concerns Persian rule.
vocabulary: An ancient length based on the forearm.
Language of God’s chosen presence and authority associated with his house.
The festival recalling Israel’s deliverance from Egypt.

notes: This ancestry connects Ezra to Aaron. Biblical genealogies can omit generations; the chain is not expanded with names from other passages.
The initial departure date is followed in 8:31 by the departure from the Ahava River on the twelfth day.
The royal letter is in Aramaic; Hebrew resumes at verse 27. The greeting in verse 12 is elliptical; “Complete greetings” supplies the implied greeting.
The word rendered “banishment” refers to removal or uprooting; its precise penalty is uncertain. The other named penalties are death, loss of property, and imprisonment.
vocabulary: A trained writer and interpreter of written instruction, not only a copyist.
A cor measured dry goods, a bath measured liquids, and a talent measured weight.
The king’s heart describes intention; God’s hand describes active help.

sections.24: The gifts entrusted to their keepers

notes: “Of the family of Shecaniah” is connected here with Hattush in verse 2. The Hebrew verse boundary falls between them.
These entries are difficult and appear incomplete: a family is named and then an unnamed “son of” Jahaziel or Josiphiah. The draft does not supply names from other textual traditions.
“The last to come” may mean the later members or remaining descendants of Adonikam.
Zaccur follows the recorded read form; the written form is Zabbud.
Sherebiah is taken here as the discerning man. The Hebrew can also be read as introducing him in addition to that man.

The draft takes Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and their ten relatives as Levites accompanying twelve leading priests, in light of verses 18–19 and 30. The compact Hebrew can also be read as a single group of twelve.
The verse names a sin offering and then calls the whole offering a burnt offering. Both statements are retained.
vocabulary: The Nethinim, assigned here to assist the Levites.
Abstaining from food as part of humbling oneself and seeking God.
Senior officials in the Persian imperial administration.

notes: “Holy seed” describes the community as offspring set apart for God. The officials use the phrase in their accusation about marriages. The text’s wording is retained without turning it into a modern racial classification.
A tent peg suggests a small but secure hold in God’s holy place. The brief respite does not end the community’s political subjection.
The protective wall is an image of security here; the verse does not establish that Jerusalem’s physical walls had already been rebuilt.
The prayer brings together themes of commands about the land and marriage. It does not quote one identifiable passage word for word.
vocabulary: A breach of an obligation or sacred trust.
Ezra describes the community’s continuing subjection even after return from exile.
Those left after disaster or judgment.

notes: “My lord” is taken as an address to Ezra. The vocalized Hebrew can be read “the Lord.” The proposal explicitly includes sending away children as well as wives; their later circumstances are not described.
Attendance was enforced by threatened loss of property and exclusion from the community.
The phrase rendered “opposed this” can also mean “stood over this,” describing responsibility for the matter. The nature of the four men’s involvement is uncertain.
The name Malchijah occurs twice in this entry; both occurrences are retained.
The Hebrew continues a long list after a second Bani heading. No additional family heading is inserted at verse 38.

The final Hebrew clause is difficult. The draft understands it to say that some of the women had borne children. Other renderings describe sending away wives with their children. This verse alone does not settle how the final action is to be expressed.
vocabulary: A binding commitment made here with God.
An acknowledgment before God; the Hebrew term can also express thanksgiving or praise.
A sacrifice connected with acknowledged liability or an offense.
